title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models

paper.title: Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube { − 1 , 1 } d \{-1,1\}^{d} , the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term. 1 1 1 Code available at https://github.com/CMcDonald-1/internal_guidance_diffusion_models

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models designed via Gaussian noising have become the dominant generative algorithm for continuous distributions [ 29 , 13 , 32 ] , and continue to show promise for discrete targets as well [ 7 , 16 , 35 ] . The original theory of diffusion models was established for unconditional generation [ 31 , 32 ] : given access to an initial pool of samples from a distribution π \pi , we train a model to sample from π \pi . As the field has matured, interest has turned towards conditional generation and tilting. Given access to only a pool of samples from π \pi , and a reward function r r , we want to train a sampling algorithm to sample from an exponential tilt by the reward function for some strength τ \tau with density π ~ ​ ( x ) ∝ π ⁡ ( x ) ​ e τ ​ r ​ ( x ) \tilde{\pi}(x)\propto\pi(x)e^{\tau r(x)} . Existing methods utilize what the authors refer to as external guidance , implementing an additive vector field called a guidance term to modify SDE paths at sampling time [ 10 , 28 , 11 ] , or a density ratio to reweight Markov chain conditional probabilities [ 33 , 24 , 17 , 12 ] . Methods such as classier-fee guidance [ 14 ] implement ad hoc and closed-form guidance terms, but are known to structurally sample the wrong invariant measure and introduce sampling artifacts such as corrupted samples and mode collapse [ 8 , 4 ] . Exact guidance schemes derive the analytically correct guidance terms, but result in an intractable object that must either be learned in an expensive neural network training run, or approximated by a tractable analog such as an empirical average that introduces compounding errors at sample time. A recent line of work [ 15 , 21 , 20 , 22 ] has opened up a new method for reward-tilted sampling we call internal guidance . Rather than modify the output of the denoiser of the base distribution with additive or multiplicative terms outside of the object, we realize we can instead shift our evaluation point inside the existing base denoiser. Recent work of Moitra et al. [21, Lemma 3.3] has shown for an internal mapping function H H we call a symmetry map, the evaluation of the denoiser of a linear tilted density is an evaluation of the base denoiser at a modified input G tilt ​ ( u , a ) = G base ​ ( u ~ = H 1 ​ ( u , a ) , a ~ = H 2 ​ ( u , a ) ) . \displaystyle G_{\text{tilt}}(u,a)=G_{\text{base}}(\tilde{u}=H_{1}(u,a),\tilde{a}=H_{2}(u,a)). These symmetry mappings are closed-form objects involving shifting and rescaling inputs, derived from the interactions of linear tilts with the quadratic log-density terms introduced via Gaussian convolution. Internal guidance has clear benefits. There is no intractable external term to approximate, and the symmetry maps H H are all explicit. A single denoising diffusion model, trained on unconditional sampling of its input distribution, is able to sample an entire family of tilted densities at inference time with no additional reinforcement learning, fine tuning, or external guidance required. The catch with this method is one of coverage. If we had access to the oracle denoiser G G we could implement such a method with no additional error over base sampling. However, we instead have a network g θ g_{\theta} trained to approximate G G . This network is only accurate in an L 2 L^{2} sense along the sequence of marginal densities produced by noising the base distribution, which we call the training manifold. The equivalent points ( u ~ , a ~ ) (\tilde{u},\tilde{a}) induced by the symmetry map represent an out-of-distribution query from the perspective of the base model denoiser, and we have no control on the accuracy of our trained network at this point. The relationship of the symmetry map can be captured by an equivalence class: for a tilted density π ~ \tilde{\pi} and an evaluation point ( u , a ) (u,a) , the equivalence class is all points ( u ~ , a ~ ) (\tilde{u},\tilde{a}) where the base denoiser evaluated at ( u ~ , a ~ ) (\tilde{u},\tilde{a}) is equal to the tilted denoiser at ( u , a ) (u,a) . The work of Moitra et al. [21] can be interpreted as showing this equivalence class exists and is non-empty, and established one symmetry map which creates the class. However, this symmetry alone is not enough to force overlap between the equivalence class of points produced by tilted sampling and the high probability region of the base distribution training manifold the denoiser network was trained on. To have equivalent points that live near the training manifold, we need to introduce additional symmetry relationships that expand the equivalence class. We restrict our study to discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube { − 1 , 1 } d \{-1,1\}^{d} , noised under continuous Gaussian convolution, and a stochastic localization algorithm to implement the reverse sampling and produce discrete outputs. The benefit of embedding in the hypercube is all discrete points are constant norm ‖ x ‖ 2 = d \|x\|^{2}=d . The conditional densities which define the denoiser are quadratic tilts to the base density which introduce linear and quadratic terms to the log-density. By the constant norm property, all quadratic terms normalize out and the denoiser is a pure linear tilt to the base density. This opens up additional symmetries that expand the equivalence class and allow modification to the training manifold. With these additional symmetries, we train a denoiser network that can be evaluated at points which are out-of-distribution from the pure noising of the base distribution, but lie in the equivalence class of points seen at sampling time. We visualize a sketch of this idea in Figure 1 . Our contributions are threefold: 1. Conditional generation tasks such as infilling and reward tilting by binary rewards can be cast as linear tilts in an extended state space by promoting the reward coordinate to an additional random variable noised and denoised when sampling. 2. We establish the theory of denoiser symmetry , the evaluation of the denoiser of a linear tilt to a base density can be recast as an evaluation of the base denoiser at a shifted evaluation point. We establish additional symmetries specific to hypercube embedded discrete distributions, by the removal of quadratic terms in the conditional log-density. 3. We introduce diagonal matrix rescalings to our hypercube embedding during training called Λ \Lambda focusing , turning an out-of-distribution learning problem into an in-distribution learning problem, and allowing the base denoiser to be evaluated at locations off the typical noising path. We demonstrate performance on small discrete sampling targets such as a non-linear reward tilt to a small 12 dimension Ising model with ground truth comparison denoiser; generating and solving 4x4, 6x6, and 9x9 Sudoku puzzles; and conditional class generation of MNIST digit images. These problems are small enough to act as a test bed where the quality of our sampling can be compared against exact ground truth values as a diagnostic of effective sampling, with future work to focus on scaling and more complex target distributions for internal guidance. Figure 1 : Sketch of denoiser symmetry. The training manifold is where the denoiser network has learned the base denoiser. The sampling manifold is the typical vectors that will be encountered when sampling a tilted density. The equivalence relationships can find a point with equal evaluation of the base denoiser near the training manifold, not all equivalence relationships map back to the region of the training manifold.

sections.text: Our sampling algorithm will be the stochastic localization path, which is equivalent to a time shifting and rescaling of the marginal densities of score-based diffusion. The benefit of stochastic localization is the drift term is exactly the denoiser, rather than being related to the score via Tweedie’s formula [ 25 ] . This makes it simpler to construct denoiser-to-denoiser relationships rather than score-to-score relationships. Definition 2 (Stochastic Localization) . sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We demonstrate the performance of the method in three experimental settings: a 12-dimensional Ising model with a non-linear reward tilt, 4x4, 6x6, and 9x9 Sudoku unconditional grid generation and puzzle solving (infilling), and MNIST conditional digit generation. Full technical descriptions of the target density, training set, model architecture, and additional details for each experiment can be found in Appendix C . All experiments are sampled up to a stochastic localization time T = 20 T=20 , with the discrete grid { t k } k = 0 K \{t_{k}\}_{k=0}^{K} is constructed with K = 1000 K=1000 and a scheduling algorithm defined in Appendix B.5 . We note that at each τ \tau tilt strength, we know the theoretical probability of producing a reward-achieving solution using the log-odds curve as discussed in Appendix B.3 .

sections.heading: 5.1 12-Dimensional Ising Model
sections.text: The 12-dimensional Ising model has a reward tilt which gives reward when the number of positive bits is exactly 10. The state space of the Ising model is small enough to enumerate giving exact ground truth for the denoiser to compare our network against. In Appendix C Figure 8 we see the network denoiser has learned the ground truth denoiser well with low L 2 L^{2} error across tilt strengths, and produces the correct proportion of reward-achieving solutions as predicted by the log-odds curve in Appendix C Figure 9 . The Ising model is a small scale experiment with ground truth denoiser to calibrate the method before proceeding to larger state spaces.

sections.heading: 5.2 4x4 Sudoku
sections.text: The 4x4 Sudoku problem has a small enough state space to enumerate the ground truth denoiser. We compare the network denoiser to the ground truth in L 2 L^{2} error in Appendix C Figure 11 , the network learns the denoiser well. For the log-odds curve in Appendix C Figure 12 we can consider the stochastic localization algorithm implemented with either the ground truth denoiser or the network estimation. Both methods track the log-odds up to 98% reward-achieving solutions at τ ≈ 3.5 \tau\approx 3.5 , but the network sampler does start to lag at higher tilt strengths while the ground truth denoiser does continue to track at high tilts up to τ = 5 \tau=5 . With 288 reward-achieving puzzles, we can track if the network is uniformly sampling these puzzles. In 3,000 generated reward-achieving puzzles, the exact-denoiser sampler visits all 288 solutions, each between 4 and 21 times, and passes a χ 2 \chi^{2} test of uniformity ( χ 287 2 = 280.1 \chi^{2}_{287}=280.1 , p = 0.60 p=0.60 ). The network visits 287 of the 288 solutions, each between 0 and 25 times, and fails the test ( χ 287 2 = 391.9 \chi^{2}_{287}=391.9 , p < 10 − 4 p<10^{-4} ). The network therefore covers nearly the whole solution set, but it does not sample it uniformly: under the reward tilt it has learned to favor some solutions over others. Results are visualized in Appendix C Figure 15 . An added benefit of embedding in the hypercube is we can do early bit-by-bit decoding of the continuous vector X t X_{t} at a time t t based on the coordinate-wise entries of the decoder | E ⁡ [ X i | X t ] | ≥ 0.75 |E[X_{i}|X_{t}]|\geq 0.75 . One of the main complaints against continuous diffusion samplers for discrete targets relative to autoregressive models and masked diffusion is that because they operate in continuous space there is no discernible discrete token string until the final decoding step. This technique solves that problem and produces a partially complete token string before terminal decoding, visualized in Appendix C Figure 13 .

sections.heading: 5.3 6x6 Sudoku
sections.text: For 6x6 Sudoku, the state space is large and there are vastly more reward-achieving puzzles than the 4x4 problem. In the 4x4 problem, the state space was size 2 32 2^{32} with only 288 reward-achieving puzzles. The training set of size 150,000 contained 5% reward-achieving puzzles indicated by a 1 in their reward coordinate. Thus each reward-achieving puzzle was seen in the training set and a memorization check was performed with a χ 2 \chi^{2} test of uniform sampling. For 6x6 Sudoku the state space is 2 108 2^{108} with 28 million reward-achieving puzzles. The training set of size 5 million contained 5% reward-achieving puzzles, which is 250,000 of the 28 million possible valid grids, 0.88%. We cannot fully enumerate the denoiser for reward tilts in the 6x6 setting, but we can show the L 2 L^{2} error for the untilted density τ = 0 \tau=0 is controlled for the learned network in Appendix C Figure 17 . The network also properly tracks the log-odds across tilt strengths in Appendix C Figure 18 . We check memorization by the rate the network reproduces a reward-achieving puzzle provided in the training set. With the training set containing 0.88 % 0.88\% of the reward-achieving puzzles, in 1,000 reward-achieving generations proper uniform sampling would produce exact matches with the training set by chance 3 3 – 14 14 with a 95 % 95\% interval. We observe 10 10 matches in 1,000 samples, consistent with no memorization.

sections.heading: 5.4 9x9 Sudoku
sections.text: For 9x9 Sudoku the state space is too large to enumerate a ground truth denoiser. The number of reward-achieving puzzles is so large there is a near 0 probability of recreating a training set puzzle under proper sampling. The training set is 10 million Sudoku grids with 5% being reward-achieving puzzles. The 9x9 Sudoku target density is the first example where the effect of self-conditioning is noticeable, self-conditioning is discussed in more detail in Appendix B.4 . In summary, we consider two modes of self-conditioning: mode “two-pass” reuses the network’s denoiser evaluation at a given time and maintains a memory one Markov structure. Mode “carry” reuses a previous time point’s denoiser value and breaks this Markov structure but is more commonly used in modern methods. The two methods give different results when tracking the log-odds in Appendix C Figures 20(a) and 20(b) . The reward coordinate is denoised jointly with the tokens, so the sampler reports its own prediction of reward in the d + 1 d+1 coordinate, and a correctly sampling model should have this prediction agree with the graded reward. The two-pass self-conditioning mode tracks the log-odds in its own reward prediction in its d + 1 d+1 coordinate, but not in the graded validity, which plateaus near 60 % 60\% . The model’s d + 1 d+1 coordinate reports it is producing reward-achieving grids far more often than it actually is. The carry self-conditioning mode plateaus near 90 % 90\% graded validity with a 8 8 – 12 % 12\% gap between predicted and graded reward. The reward function is very sharp, mis-sampling a single bit gives 0 reward. Sampled non-reward grids are typically close to reward ones: 90 % 90\% of two-pass samples lie within 10 10 out of 324 324 bits of the nearest valid grid in Hamming distance (Appendix C Figure 21 ), consistent with a few bits mis-sampled late in the trajectory being penalized by the sharp validity reward. The model performs both unconditional grid generation and infilling, which some may call “solving” a puzzle, by adding a cell-fixing tilt to the reward tilt (Figure 3 ). This type of sampling is natural for the diffusion model here which operates under linear tilts and decodes in any order, but would be difficult for a left-to-right autoregressive model which would need to backtrack against later given values. We use a reward tilt strength and infill tilt strength of τ = 3 \tau=3 and carry self-condition mode across various numbers of given cell values in Appendix C Table 1 and Figure 4 . Note the sampler may not maintain the initial given cell values as they are a tilt vector not a hard constraint. Given 71 / 81 71/81 cells the model maintains the initial cells and achieved reward in 100 % 100\% of 2000 2000 draws. Given 11 / 81 11/81 cells, the initial cell values are maintained 92 % 92\% of the time, a reward achieved 87 % 87\% of the time, and both objectives satisfied 80 % 80\% of the time. Finally, the model has no indication of memorizing the training set. Of 1000 1000 unconditional draws at τ = 3 \tau=3 none match the training set. Splitting the training set into two halves, the cell-wise Hamming distance from each reward-achieving sample to its nearest reference grid in one half has the same distribution as that of sample from the split training set half in Appendix Figure 23 . Model produced reward-achieving puzzles are novel and no more similar than a two part split of training points to themselves. (a) Unconditional generation from a blank grid. (b) Conditional generation from a partially given puzzle. Figure 3 : Sudoku 9x9 completions sampled from the tilt-operator network. Figure 4 : Probability of correct grid infilling across input cell numbers. Given no initial cells, should return a valid grid 95% of the time, we measure saturation at 87% without any infilling.

sections.heading: 5.5 MNIST Digit Images
sections.text: The MNIST data set consists of 60,000 images of hand drawn digits 0-9 and 10,000 hold out examples. We encode reward as a 10 10 -bit one-hot class block, and generating class tilts along the whole block with 1 class being positively tilted and the other 9 negatively tilted. Generated images are classified by an independent CNN classifier ( 98.74 % 98.74\% held-out accuracy). Since the scorer has a ceiling to its classifier accuracy, the observable success rate saturates at the classifier’s per-class sensitivity; points beyond τ ≈ 1.69 \tau\approx 1.69 are uninformative. In Appendix C Figure 29 we see generated pools of images show similar variety and quality as hold out examples not used for training indicating no mode collapse or degradation of digit quality under tilting. In Appendix C Figures 24 - 27 self-conditioning mode two-pass and carry are also compared for their tracking of the log-odds. In this experiment, carry mode seems to over-sample a class at medium tilts. Two-pass tracks the classifier-corrected exact rate within its confidence interval through τ ≈ 1 \tau\approx 1 , in both the classifier score and the network’s own reward block. Carry overshoots the tilt in every class: at τ = 0.51 \tau=0.51 it produces the requested class 57.8 % 57.8\% of the time against an exact 45.9 % 45.9\% , with the 95 % 95\% interval excluding the exact value at every τ \tau from 0.26 0.26 to 1.03 1.03 . Both methods produce 95% class correct images at large tilts, and further tilt strengths go beyond the judge CNN’s sensitivity.

sections.heading: B.2 Stochastic Localization
sections.text: Stochastic localization can be viewed as a different time scaling and spatial scaling than the usual score-based diffusion derived from the forwards flow Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as outlined in Montanari [23] . We re-derive the equivalence here for an audience more familiar with the score-based construction. The score-based diffusion is variance preserving, initialized at a standard normal draw, and uses the score as its drift. The stochastic localization process is not variance preserving (it is growing in magnitude over time), is initialized at a Dirac mass at the origin, and uses the denoiser as its drift term. Both can be derived from the same reverse diffusion process theory.

By the time-reversal result of Anderson [1] , popularized in modern literature by Song et al. [32] , Lipman et al. [19] , consider any target density π \pi and initialize X 0 ∼ π X_{0}\sim\pi . sections.heading: Model-reported reward.
sections.text: Since the reward coordinate is denoised jointly with the token coordinates, the sampler also produces an internal prediction of reward: the sign of the terminal d + 1 d+1 coordinate, or the argmax of the class block. For a correctly sampling model this prediction and the externally graded reward agree in expectation. Comparing the two curves against the exact line separates two failure modes: a gap between the internal prediction and the exact line indicates the sampler does not produce the tilted marginal on the reward coordinate; a gap between the internal prediction and the graded reward indicates the token coordinates are inconsistent with the reward coordinate produced. The 9x9 Sudoku two-pass and carry results in Appendix C are distinguished by this comparison.

sections.heading: B.4 Self-Conditioning
sections.text: Self-conditioning as originally introduced in Chen et al. [7] is a method to improve the sample quality of a denoising diffusion model. It was originally derived as a mostly ad hoc engineering decision, rather than a method arising from sound theory. Its interaction with standard theory for error control for diffusion models has not yet been fully understood [ 30 , 18 , 6 , 5 , 3 , 9 , 34 ] . In this paper we consider two forms of self-conditioning: one method we call mode “two-pass” is a Markovian form of self-conditioning, it uses only information available at a given time point of a discrete diffusion to estimate the denoiser as in Algorithm 6 in Chen et al. [7] . This method can be considered an architecture choice for the denoiser estimator network and is compatible with existing diffusion model error control theory which views the reverse process as a Euler-Maruyama discretization of the continuous SDE with pointwise denoiser estimation. The second method of self-conditioning we call mode “carry” is when the denoiser reuses its previous estimate at time t − 1 t-1 to make its denoiser estimate at time t t . This is the more common method implemented in modern denoising diffusion models, however it breaks the memory-one Markov structure under which diffusion model error control theory is currently understood. The denoiser is a conditional expectation on the origin point of a noisy observation given partial information provided by the noised observation, F ⁡ ( u , a ) = E π ​ [ X | U = a ​ X + 1 − a 2 ​ Z ] . \displaystyle F(u,a)=E_{\pi}[X|U=aX+\sqrt{1-a^{2}}Z]. sections.heading: C.2 4x4 Sudoku
sections.text: Target Density 4 × 4 4\times 4 Sudoku has a state space of size 2 32 2^{32} , with only 288 valid puzzles which satisfy row, column and box constraints. Each cell is a 2 2 -bit encoding of the numbers 1 1 – 4 4 with no dead code words, so the 16 cells give exactly 32 bits and every bit string decodes to a grid. Figure 10 : Example valid 4x4 grid. The base distribution is a weak generator sampling each row independently. With probability 1 − ρ 1-\rho it makes the row a uniformly random permutation of the numbers 1 1 – 4 4 , and thus a valid row; with probability ρ \rho it instead draws the row’s 8 bits uniformly at random, giving any of the 256 possible rows. We use ρ = 0.02 \rho=0.02 . A single row is therefore valid with probability ( 1 − ρ ) + ρ ⋅ 24 256 = 98.19 % (1-\rho)+\rho\cdot\frac{24}{256}=98.19\% , and all four rows are simultaneously valid 92.94 % 92.94\% of the time. The generator has no knowledge of column or box constraints, however, so it produces a proper puzzle only 0.081 % 0.081\% of the time by chance. The reward is the indicator of a valid puzzle appended as a 33rd coordinate, giving the extended state space { − 1 , 1 } 33 \{-1,1\}^{33} . Training Set Because a proper puzzle arises by chance only 0.081 % 0.081\% of the time, the base distribution is mixed with an injection component: each sample is drawn from the uniform distribution over the 288 valid solutions with probability p inject = 0.05 p_{\text{inject}}=0.05 , and from the weak generator otherwise. The training set consists of 150,000 samples drawn from this mixture, of which in expectation 142,500 come from the weak generator and 7,500 are injected proper Sudoku puzzles. The resulting exact reward probability is 5.08 % 5.08\% ; the realized training file contains 7,590 genuinely valid grids ( 5.06 % 5.06\% ). Model Architecture The operator network is the same residual MLP with mean-field skip connection used for the Ising experiment, G θ ​ ( u , a ) = tanh ⁡ ( β ⁡ ( a ) ​ u + g θ ​ ( a ) ⊙ r θ ​ ( u , a ) ) , \displaystyle G_{\theta}(u,a)=\tanh\!\big(\beta(a)\,u+g_{\theta}(a)\odot r_{\theta}(u,a)\big), scaled up for the larger state space. The signal level enters through a 10-dimensional level embedding e ⁡ ( a ) = [ a , log ⁡ ( 1 + β ⁡ ( a ) ) , sin ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ a ​ f ) , cos ⁡ ( 2 ​ π ​ a ​ f ) ] e(a)=[\,a,\ \log(1+\beta(a)),\ \sin(2\pi af),\ \cos(2\pi af)\,] with Fourier frequencies f ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } f\in\{1,2,4,8\} . The input u ∈ ℝ 33 u\in\mathbb{R}^{33} is scaled by 1 / d 1/\sqrt{d} , concatenated with e ⁡ ( a ) e(a) , and mapped by a linear layer to width 1024, followed by 8 pre-activation residual blocks, each consisting of LayerNorm, FiLM modulation ( 1 + g k ) ​ LN ​ ( h ) + b k (1+g_{k})\,\mathrm{LN}(h)+b_{k} with ( g k , b k ) (g_{k},b_{k}) predicted from e ⁡ ( a ) e(a) , and two width-1024 linear layers with SiLU activations. A final LayerNorm and linear layer project to the 33 output coordinates, and a separate gain head ( 10 → 32 → 33 10\to 32\to 33 , SiLU) predicts the per-coordinate gain g θ ​ ( a ) g_{\theta}(a) . The output layer is zero-initialized so training begins exactly at the mean-field prediction. The model has 17,072,582 17{,}072{,}582 parameters. Full implementation details are in the supplementary code. Training Run The model was trained for 30,000 Adam steps with batch size 8192, learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and a cosine-annealing learning rate schedule over the full 30,000 steps. Each batch re-noises freshly drawn training samples, with β \beta drawn log-uniformly on [ 0.02 , 50 ] [0.02,50] . Two focusing profiles are mixed per row: with probability 0.25 0.25 the row uses the sparse infill profile, in which k k is drawn uniformly on { 2 , … , 32 } \{2,\dots,32\} and a random k k -subset of the core coordinates is set to 32 / k \sqrt{32/k} with the rest zeroed, and otherwise it uses the reward-focusing profile. Independently, the reward-axis stretch λ \lambda is set to 1 with probability 0.25 0.25 and otherwise drawn log-uniformly on [ 1 , 5 ] [1,5] . Both profiles preserve the budget identity ∑ i Λ i ​ i 2 = d \sum_{i}\Lambda_{ii}^{2}=d , so the operator being learned is unchanged. Processing 30,000 × 8192 ≈ 2.46 × 10 8 30{,}000\times 8192\approx 2.46\times 10^{8} samples through a 17,072,582 17{,}072{,}582 -parameter network corresponds to approximately 2.5 × 10 16 2.5\times 10^{16} training FLOPs under the standard 6 ​ N ​ D 6ND estimate. Extended Results For the 4x4 Sudoku problem, the reward set is only 288 valid grids, and the weak generator decomposes into a product measure across rows. As such, the ground truth denoiser can be computed via enumeration at any reward tilt strength. The estimated L 2 L^{2} error across tilt strength is shown in Figure 11 . The denoiser error does increase with τ \tau tilt strength, but does have a uniform bound across tilt and signal levels of 0.5 0.5 . We show the actual 33 values of the base denoiser E [ X i | u , a ] E[X_{i}|u,a] and learned network for 5 sampled u u values from a τ = 0 \tau=0 draw and a τ = 4 \tau=4 draw in Figure 14 . Expected values are all between − 1 -1 and 1 1 . Note the τ = 0 \tau=0 draws are all noisy versions of non-reward-achieving solutions, and the 33rd coordinate (the reward coordinate) accurately assigns them all a -1. The 5 τ = 4 \tau=4 draws are noisy reward-achieving solutions and the 33rd coordinate assigns them all a +1 value. The untilted τ = 0 \tau=0 network achieves near 0 error on these examples and is visually indistinguishable. The τ = 4 \tau=4 network is still very good, but is noticeably a bit off on a few coordinates, which agrees with the average increase in squared error seen in Figure 11 . Figure 11 : Comparison of L 2 L^{2} error of learned denoiser of 4x4 Sudoku problem across tilt strengths. For the 4x4 Sudoku problem we have access to the ground truth denoiser and the net estimated denoiser. Thus we can run stochastic localization with exact denoiser evaluations and with network approximated denoiser evaluation and track the error introduced by incorrect denoiser evaluations isolated from discretization error. To track the log-odds in Figure 12 , we compute the τ \tau that would achieve 98% reward if sampled correctly. We then look at 5 τ \tau levels before this value and 5 levels after up to maximum tilt value strength d + 1 = 5.74 \sqrt{d+1}=5.74 . Note all levels past the dashed line should be achieving reward more than 98% of the time. Confidence intervals are computed using a Clopper-Pearson method which often includes 100% reward as an upper bound. The localization samples using the ground truth denoiser tracks the log-odds across all levels, even past 98% when considering the confidence intervals from 2000 samples. The network based sampler tracks well up to the 98% level, but then does strictly under-sample past this high bar with the confidence intervals not overlapping the theoretical log-odds. Note when the network based sampler fails to exactly track the log-odds at this high tilt it is still generating over 98% reward-achieving puzzles, but still under-sampling its theoretical value at this tilt. Figure 12 : 4x4 Sudoku log-odds across tilt strengths. As an added bonus to the stochastic localization path, the denoiser E ⁡ [ X i | X t ] E[X_{i}|X_{t}] acts as both the drift term and a prediction of the terminal sign of a given coordinate. As such, if a coordinate ever passes a threshold | E ⁡ [ X i | X t ] | > ℓ |E[X_{i}|X_{t}]|>\ell , we can consider that bit “confident” and fix that bit to the sign of the denoiser at that moment. This allows for “early decoding” seeing which bits the network fixes in which order and at what point of the trajectory. Note a bit is allowed to flip signs, all that is decoded is the terminal sign value. Fixed bits determine what tokens (cell values) are still valid among the unfixed bits. One of the arguments against continuous diffusion for discrete targets is that the trajectory remains a continuous value that cannot be interpreted in discrete token space until the terminal decoding step, unlike masked diffusion or autoregressive models which build partial discrete token strings along their trajectory. By using the confidence based bit decoding, we can achieve a similar effect to see what discrete set of tokens the puzzle was considering at each moment in the trajectory and soft decode at any time. When both bits in a cell are fixed we record the cell value, when one bit is fixed such as ( ∗ , − 1 ) (*,-1) this means the cell will get either a ( 1 , − 1 CLOSE (1,-1 ) which is token 2 or ( − 1 − 1 ) (-1-1) which is token 1. We record this with Sudoku “pencil marks” showing what is considered still possible in the cell. We note the network is not “solving” the puzzle “logically” as a human would by applying row, column, and box constraints in sequence. For example, in the second frozen grid in Figure 13 , there is a 1 fixed in the bottom left box. This would rule out all 1’s in that column, but the upper box cells in the same column have not yet ruled out a 1 in that column since the bits for those two cells have not yet reached their own confidence level. This is therefore a sequence of most likely puzzles tracking the most confident bits at each moment in the trajectory. We call this path a “fuzzy trajectory” tracking the denoiser coordinate values across the signal levels, noting when a coordinate achieves a confidence level more than 0.75 in magnitude, and recording events when a cell gets fixed in Figure 13 . Note some cells do become confident but ultimately flip their token value by the end of the run. Note the row 2 column 4 cell flips from a 2 to a 4 by the end of sampling. We run our stochastic localization up to a T T value of 20 20 but the network has mostly decided on its final value much earlier by time T = 3 T=3 it would seem. Figure 13 : Sudoku 4x4 denoiser trajectory and early decoding. Partially complete discrete token sequences fixed when denoiser coordinates pass magnitude threshold. (a) (b) Figure 14 : Example ground truth denoiser and network denoiser in 33 coordinates at sampled points. Samples in a) are untilted sampled and b) tilted samples. sections.text: Target Density 6 × 6 6\times 6 Sudoku has 6 rows, 6 columns, and six non-overlapping 2 × 3 2\times 3 rectangular boxes, each of which must be a permutation of 1 1 – 6 6 to be valid. Each cell is a 3 3 -bit encoding of the numbers 1 1 – 6 6 , giving 36 × 3 = 108 36\times 3=108 core bits and a state space of 2 108 2^{108} . Unlike the 4 × 4 4\times 4 case, this encoding has dead code words : three bits admit eight values, of which only six are legal, so two codes per cell decode to the invalid values 7 7 and 8 8 . The generator never emits them, but the model operates on the full 2 108 2^{108} space and can. Figure 16 : Example valid 6x6 grid. There are 28,200,960 28{,}200{,}960 proper puzzles, vastly more than the 4x4 puzzle. The training set does not contain all proper puzzles, thus the network’s generations should be novel making new proper puzzles not seen in the training set. The base distribution is again a weak generator sampling each row independently. With probability 1 − ρ 1-\rho the row is a uniformly random permutation of 1 1 – 6 6 , and thus valid; with probability ρ \rho it is instead six i.i.d. uniform digits drawn from 1 1 – 6 6 , which may repeat. We use ρ = 0.02 \rho=0.02 . A row is therefore valid with probability ( 1 − ρ ) + ρ ⋅ 720 6 6 = 98.03 % (1-\rho)+\rho\cdot\frac{720}{6^{6}}=98.03\% , and all six rows are simultaneously valid 88.75 % 88.75\% of the time. Because the generator enforces no column or box constraints, and the grid is much larger than in the 4 × 4 4\times 4 case, it produces a proper puzzle with probability only 1.8 × 10 − 10 1.8\times 10^{-10} — effectively never. The reward is again the validity indicator. Training Set Since the weak generator essentially never produces a proper puzzle on its own, reward-achieving examples must be injected: each sample is drawn uniformly from the set of valid solutions with probability p inject = 0.05 p_{\text{inject}}=0.05 , and from the weak generator otherwise. The training is scaled up to 5,000,000 5{,}000{,}000 samples from this mixture, roughly 33 times larger than the 4 × 4 4\times 4 training set, which is necessary because the injected solutions are drawn from a pool of 28.2 28.2 million rather than 288 288 . The realized set contains 249,903 249{,}903 valid grids ( 5.00 % 5.00\% ), of which 248,778 248{,}778 are distinct. Model Architecture The target distributions and models were trained in order from smallest to largest state space starting with the Ising Model, then 4x4, 6x6, 9x9 Sudoku, then the MNIST problem. As the state space scaled up in size, larger data sets were needed to learn the more complicated density and tilt, and more expressive model architectures. The previous Ising and 4x4 Sudoku problems used MLP models with no attention mechanism. For 6x6, 9x9 Sudoku and MNIST we use a transformer architecture with attention. This problem uses a transformer featurizer rather than the residual MLP, since the row, column and box constraints are joint combinatorial structure that a flat trunk must discover entirely from data, whereas attention can relate cells directly. The 108 core bits are split into 6 tokens of 18 bits (one per row), and the reward coordinate is given its own token rather than folded into the level conditioning, so attention can relate x ∗ x_{*} to every row and vice versa; attention is non-causal over the resulting 7 slots. The model has 4 4 layers with d model = 256 d_{\text{model}}=256 , 8 8 attention heads, and feed-forward dimension 1024 1024 , and noise-level conditioning enters by AdaLN from the same Fourier level embedding e ⁡ ( a ) e(a) used elsewhere. The output head is unchanged, preserving the mean-field skip G θ ​ ( u , a ) = tanh ⁡ ( β ⁡ ( a ) ​ u + g θ ​ ( a ) ⊙ r θ ​ ( u , a ) ) , \displaystyle G_{\theta}(u,a)=\tanh\!\big(\beta(a)\,u+g_{\theta}(a)\odot r_{\theta}(u,a)\big), with every residual branch zero-initialized so that at initialization the network is exactly the mean-field denoiser. The network is additionally self-conditioned, as discussed in Appendix B.4 , the previous estimate of x 0 x_{0} is concatenated to the input along the feature axis of each token, doubling the per-slot input channels from 18 to 36. The model has 3,249,028 3{,}249{,}028 parameters, substantially fewer than the 4 × 4 4\times 4 MLP despite the much larger state space. Full implementation details are in the supplementary code. Training Run The model was trained for 180,000 Adam steps with batch size 8192, learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and a cosine-annealing schedule over the full 180,000 steps. During training the self-conditioning input is supplied with probability 0.5 0.5 , so the network also learns the zero-input fallback needed at the first sampling step. Each batch re-noises freshly drawn samples, with β \beta drawn log-uniformly on [ 0.02 , 50 ] [0.02,50] ; with probability 0.3 0.3 the row instead draws β \beta log-uniformly from the narrower band [ 0.5 , 2.5 ] [0.5,2.5] , which over-samples the regime empirically hardest to fit. With probability 0.25 0.25 a row uses the sparse infill profile ( k k uniform on { 2 , … , 108 } \{2,\dots,108\} , a random k k -subset set to 108 / k \sqrt{108/k} ), and otherwise the reward-focusing profile; independently, the reward-axis stretch λ \lambda is 1 1 with probability 0.25 0.25 and otherwise log-uniform on [ 1 , 10 ] [1,10] . Each cell is a 4 4 -bit encoding of the numbers 1 1 – 9 9 , giving 81 × 4 = 324 81\times 4=324 core bits and a state space of 2 324 2^{324} . The base distribution is again a weak generator sampling each row independently: with probability 1 − ρ 1-\rho a uniformly random permutation of 1 1 – 9 9 , and with probability ρ \rho nine i.i.d. uniform digits from 1 1 – 9 9 , which may repeat. We use ρ = 0.02 \rho=0.02 , giving a row validity of 98.00 % 98.00\% and all nine rows simultaneously valid 83.39 % 83.39\% of the time. With no column or box constraints enforced, the generator produces a proper puzzle with probability 5.1 × 10 − 29 5.1\times 10^{-29} . The reward is the validity indicator, appended as a 325th coordinate to give the extended state space { − 1 , 1 } 325 \{-1,1\}^{325} . Signal levels are drawn log-uniformly on [ 0.02 , 50 ] [0.02,50] , with probability 0.3 0.3 instead drawn from the harder band [ 0.5 , 2.5 ] [0.5,2.5] . With probability 0.25 0.25 a row uses the sparse infill profile ( k k uniform on { 2 , … , 324 } \{2,\dots,324\} , a random k k -subset set to 324 / k \sqrt{324/k} ), and otherwise the reward-focusing profile; the reward-axis stretch λ \lambda is 1 1 with probability 0.25 0.25 and otherwise log-uniform on [ 1 , 17 ] [1,17] . Training ran on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 GPU (Hopper, CUDA 12.6) on the PSC Bridges-2 cluster and took 22.5 hours. sections.heading: C.5 MNIST Conditional Image Generation
sections.text: Target Density MNIST consists of 28 × 28 28\times 28 grayscale images of handwritten digits 0 0 – 9 9 , with pixel intensities in { 0 , … , 255 } \{0,\dots,255\} . Each pixel is encoded with 8 8 bits, giving 784 × 8 = 6,272 784\times 8=6{,}272 core bits and a state space of 2 6272 2^{6272} . Since the pixel values have a natural ordering, we use a Gray code encoding for each pixel, so that adjacent intensity levels differ in exactly one bit. Since there are 10 digit classes, the reward is a 10 10 -bit block rather than a single coordinate. The class label c c is stored as a one-hot pattern r c ∈ { − 1 , 1 } 10 r_{c}\in\{-1,1\}^{10} , + 1 +1 in position c c and − 1 -1 elsewhere, appended to the image bits to give the extended state space { − 1 , 1 } 6282 \{-1,1\}^{6282} . To generate class c c we tilt along the whole pattern, h = τ ​ r c h=\tau\,r_{c} , rather than along the single axis e c e_{c} . Thus one class receives a positive tilt while the others all receive a negative one. This causes the log-odds of a class to have a slope of 4, logit ⁡ π τ ​ ( c ) = logit ⁡ π ⁡ ( c ) + 4 ​ τ , \displaystyle\operatorname{logit}\pi_{\tau}(c)=\operatorname{logit}\pi(c)+4\tau, where π ⁡ ( c ) \pi(c) is the training-set frequency of class c c ( 0.090 0.090 – 0.112 0.112 ). The slope is 4 4 rather than the slope 2 2 of the single-bit reward tilt in the Sudoku and Ising problems. Training Set The training set is the standard 60,000 60{,}000 MNIST training images and their labels, each encoded as above. The official 10,000 10{,}000 -image test split is held out and never used for training. It is used for three things: (i) a fixed batch of 4,096 4{,}096 held-out images, noised with the training recipe, is scored every 1,000 1{,}000 steps to monitor overfitting; (ii) it provides the real-digit comparison in Figure 28 ; and (iii) it is used to measure the error rates of the classifier that scores generated samples (see Extended Results). Model Architecture We use the same self-conditioned transformer as for 6 × 6 6\times 6 and 9 × 9 9\times 9 Sudoku, with tokens built from image patches. The image is divided into a 7 × 7 7\times 7 grid of non-overlapping 4 × 4 4\times 4 pixel patches. Each patch becomes one token of 16 × 8 = 128 16\times 8=128 bits (pixels in row order within a patch, Gray bits most significant first), giving 49 49 image tokens. The 10 10 -bit class block is given its own token, and non-causal attention runs over the resulting 50 50 slots. The model has 4 4 layers with d model = 256 d_{\text{model}}=256 , 8 8 attention heads, and feed-forward dimension 1024 1024 , with AdaLN noise-level conditioning from the Fourier level embedding e ⁡ ( a ) e(a) and the same zero-initialized mean-field skip G θ ​ ( u , a ) = tanh ⁡ ( β ⁡ ( a ) ​ u + g θ ​ ( a ) ⊙ r θ ​ ( u , a ) ) . \displaystyle G_{\theta}(u,a)=\tanh\!\big(\beta(a)\,u+g_{\theta}(a)\odot r_{\theta}(u,a)\big). Self-conditioning concatenates the previous x 0 x_{0} estimate to each token’s features, doubling the per-slot input channels from 128 128 to 256 256 . The model has 3,555,256 3{,}555{,}256 parameters. Full implementation details are in the supplementary code. Training Run The model was trained for 30,000 30{,}000 Adam steps with batch size 2048 2048 , learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , and a cosine-annealing schedule, with the self-conditioning input supplied with probability 0.5 0.5 . Signal levels are drawn log-uniformly on β ∈ [ 0.02 , 50 ] \beta\in[0.02,50] . Λ \Lambda focusing is applied to the whole 10-bit reward block, maintaining the sign of those inputs but increasing their magnitude. The λ \lambda is 1 1 with probability 0.25 0.25 and otherwise log-uniform on [ 1 , 24 ] [1,24] . The upper limit differs from the Sudoku runs: because the whole 10 10 -coordinate block is stretched at once, the admissible range is λ < d / 10 = 25.06 \lambda<\sqrt{d/10}=25.06 rather than d \sqrt{d} , and we train just below this limit. 30,000 × 2048 ≈ 6.1 × 10 7 30{,}000\times 2048\approx 6.1\times 10^{7} draws amount to roughly 1,000 1{,}000 passes over the 60,000 60{,}000 training images. The held-out loss decreased steadily from 720.6 720.6 at step 1,000 1{,}000 to 632.1 632.1 at step 30,000 30{,}000 and was still flat-to-decreasing at the end. This gives no sign of overfitting. Training ran on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU on the PSC Bridges-2 cluster for 1 hour and 15 minutes. Processing 6.1 × 10 7 6.1\times 10^{7} samples through a 3,555,256 3{,}555{,}256 -parameter network corresponds to approximately 1.3 × 10 15 1.3\times 10^{15} training FLOPs under the standard 6 ​ N ​ D 6ND estimate. Extended Results To detect if a generated image is of a given class, we train an independent score CNN classifier. The scorer is a two-layer CNN (1.2M parameters) trained for 3 epochs with Adam on the 60,000 MNIST training images, reaching 98.74% accuracy on the held-out test split. The classifier is an imperfect instrument and cannot detect very strong tilt accuracies beyond its own classification error. Its error is also not constant across classes. As such, our ability to detect tilt strength saturates at the classifier accuracy. Near the top of the tilt range its error is the dominant source of uncertainty. Let s c s_{c} be the probability the classifier labels a true class- c c image as c c , and e c e_{c} the probability it labels an image of another class as c c . For a true class- c c rate p p , the rate we observe is m = p ​ s c + ( 1 − p ) ​ e c . \displaystyle m=p\,s_{c}+(1-p)\,e_{c}. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube { − 1 , 1 } d \{-1,1\}^{d} , the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term. 1 1 1 Code available at https://github.com/CMcDonald-1/internal_guidance_diffusion_models 1 Introduction Diffusion models designed via Gaussian noising have become the dominant generative algorithm for continuous distributions [ 29 , 13 , 32 ] , and continue to show promise for discrete targets as well [ 7 , 16 , 35 ] . The original theory of diffusion models was established for unconditional generation [ 31 , 32 ] : given access to an initial pool of samples from a distribution π \pi , we train a model to sample from π \pi . As the field has matured, interest has turned towards conditional generation and tilting. Given access to only a pool of samples from π \pi , and a reward function r r , we want to train a sampling algorithm to sample from an exponential tilt by the reward function for some strength τ \tau with density π ~ ​ ( x ) ∝ π ⁡ ( x ) ​ e τ ​ r ​ ( x ) \tilde{\pi}(x)\propto\pi(x)e^{\tau r(x)} . Existing methods utilize what the authors refer to as external guidance , implementing an additive vector field called a guidance term to modify SDE paths at sampling time [ 10 , 28 , 11 ] , or a density ratio to reweight Markov chain conditional probabilities [ 33 , 24 , 17 , 12 ] . Methods such as classier-fee guidance [ 14 ] implement ad hoc and closed-form guidance terms, but are known to structurally sample the wrong invariant measure and introduce sampling artifacts such as corrupted samples and mode collapse [ 8 , 4 ] . Exact guidance schemes derive the analytically correct guidance terms, but result in an intractable object that must either be learned in an expensive neural network training run, or approximated by a tractable analog such as an empirical average that introduces compounding errors at sample time. A recent line of work [ 15 , 21 , 20 , 22 ] has opened up a new method for reward-tilted sampling we call internal guidance . Rather than modify the output of the denoiser of the base distribution with additive or multiplicative terms outside of the object, we realize we can instead shift our evaluation point inside the existing base denoiser. Recent work of Moitra et al. [21, Lemma 3.3] has shown for an internal mapping function H H we call a symmetry map, the evaluation of the denoiser of a linear tilted density is an evaluation of the base denoiser at a modified input G tilt ​ ( u , a ) = G base ​ ( u ~ = H 1 ​ ( u , a ) , a ~ = H 2 ​ ( u , a ) ) . \displaystyle G_{\text{tilt}}(u,a)=G_{\text{base}}(\tilde{u}=H_{1}(u,a),\tilde{a}=H_{2}(u,a)). These symmetry mappings are closed-form objects involving shifting and rescaling inputs, derived from the interactions of linear tilts with the quadratic log-density terms introduced via Gaussian convolution. Internal guidance has clear benefits. There is no intractable external term to approximate, and the symmetry maps H H are all explicit. A single denoising diffusion model, trained on unconditional sampling of its input distribution, is able to sample an entire family of tilted densities at inference time with no additional reinforcement learning, fine tuning, or external guidance required. The catch with this method is one of coverage. If we had access to the oracle denoiser G G we could implement such a method with no additional error over base sampling. However, we instead have a network g θ g_{\theta} trained to approximate G G . This network is only accurate in an L 2 L^{2} sense along the sequence of marginal densities produced by noising the base distribution, which we call the training manifold. The equivalent points ( u ~ , a ~ ) (\tilde{u},\tilde{a}) induced by the symmetry map represent an out-of-distribution query from the perspective of the base model denoiser, and we have no control on the accuracy of our trained network at this point. The relationship of the symmetry map can be captured by an equivalence class: for a tilted density π ~ \tilde{\pi} and an evaluation point ( u , a ) (u,a) , the equivalence class is all points ( u ~ , a ~ ) (\tilde{u},\tilde{a}) where the base denoiser evaluated at ( u ~ , a ~ ) (\tilde{u},\tilde{a}) is equal to the tilted denoiser at ( u , a ) (u,a) . The work of Moitra et al. [21] can be interpreted as showing this equivalence class exists and is non-empty, and established one symmetry map which creates the class. However, this symmetry alone is not enough to force overlap between the equivalence class of points produced by tilted sampling and the high probability region of the base distribution training manifold the denoiser network was trained on. To have equivalent points that live near the training manifold, we need to introduce additional symmetry relationships that expand the equivalence class. We restrict our study to discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube { − 1 , 1 } d \{-1,1\}^{d} , noised under continuous Gaussian convolution, and a stochastic localization algorithm to implement the reverse sampling and produce discrete outputs. The benefit of embedding in the hypercube is all discrete points are constant norm ‖ x ‖ 2 = d \|x\|^{2}=d . The conditional densities which define the denoiser are quadratic tilts to the base density which introduce linear and quadratic terms to the log-density. By the constant norm property, all quadratic terms normalize out and the denoiser is a pure linear tilt to the base density. This opens up additional symmetries that expand the equivalence class and allow modification to the training manifold. With these additional symmetries, we train a denoiser network that can be evaluated at points which are out-of-distribution from the pure noising of the base distribution, but lie in the equivalence class of points seen at sampling time. We visualize a sketch of this idea in Figure 1 . Our contributions are threefold: 1. Conditional generation tasks such as infilling and reward tilting by binary rewards can be cast as linear tilts in an extended state space by promoting the reward coordinate to an additional random variable noised and denoised when sampling. 2. We establish the theory of denoiser symmetry , the evaluation of the denoiser of a linear tilt to a base density can be recast as an evaluation of the base denoiser at a shifted evaluation point. We establish additional symmetries specific to hypercube embedded discrete distributions, by the removal of quadratic terms in the conditional log-density. 3. We introduce diagonal matrix rescalings to our hypercube embedding during training called Λ \Lambda focusing , turning an out-of-distribution learning problem into an in-distribution learning problem, and allowing the base denoiser to be evaluated at locations off the typical noising path. We demonstrate performance on small discrete sampling targets such as a non-linear reward tilt to a small 12 dimension Ising model with ground truth comparison denoiser; generating and solving 4x4, 6x6, and 9x9 Sudoku puzzles; and conditional class generation of MNIST digit images. These problems are small enough to act as a test bed where the quality of our sampling can be compared against exact ground truth values as a diagnostic of effective sampling, with future work to focus on scaling and more complex target distributions for internal guidance. In summary, we consider two modes of self-conditioning: mode “two-pass” reuses the network’s denoiser evaluation at a given time and maintains a memory one Markov structure. Mode “carry” reuses a previous time point’s denoiser value and breaks this Markov structure but is more commonly used in modern methods. The two methods give different results when tracking the log-odds in Appendix C Figures 20(a) and 20(b) . The reward coordinate is denoised jointly with the tokens, so the sampler reports its own prediction of reward in the d + 1 d+1 coordinate, and a correctly sampling model should have this prediction agree with the graded reward. The two-pass self-conditioning mode tracks the log-odds in its own reward prediction in its d + 1 d+1 coordinate, but not in the graded validity, which plateaus near 60 % 60\% . The model’s d + 1 d+1 coordinate reports it is producing reward-achieving grids far more often than it actually is. The carry self-conditioning mode plateaus near 90 % 90\% graded validity with a 8 8 – 12 % 12\% gap between predicted and graded reward. The reward function is very sharp, mis-sampling a single bit gives 0 reward.
